implementation_notes: Default realization: declare version_id_col on the aggregate root's mapper and nothing on the members, so the ORM emits UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND version_id = :old and raises StaleDataError when the cluster changed since it was loaded. One token declared in the mapper replaces per-member version columns and lock rows, and a server-side generator (PostgreSQL xmin, version_id_generator=False) keeps the token honest. It applies to the flush path only - bulk Query.update()/delete() bypass it - so member writes must go through the ORM object graph or bump the root explicitly.

variants.code_sketch:
class Order(Base):                    # aggregate root
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(nullable=False)
    __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}

root = session.get(Order, order_id)
root.lines[0].qty += 1              # any member change
session.commit()                    # StaleDataError if cluster changed
pitfalls: The version column must not be NULL and must be touched by the root's UPDATE; a member-only write that misses the root leaves the guard silent.
Session identity-map caching can return stale members after a conflict; expire or use a fresh Session when retrying, or the same version is checked again.

variants.name: with_for_update() on the root query
variants.implementation_notes: Pessimistic realization: load the root with select(Order).where(...).with_for_update() (or Query.with_for_update()) inside a transaction, which renders SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (or the dialect's equivalent) and holds that row lock until commit. Every member touched afterwards is covered by the root lock, and a single lock identity replaces per-member locking; the standard knobs - nowait, skip_locked, of - control what happens when the root is already locked.
variants.code_sketch:
with Session(engine) as session, session.begin():
    root = session.execute(
        select(Order).where(Order.id == order_id).with_for_update()
    ).scalar_one()
    for line in root.lines:          # covered by the root lock
        line.qty += delta
# lock released when the transaction ends
pitfalls: with_for_update() outside an explicit transaction is pointless: autocommit releases the lock immediately, so the next statement is unprotected.
On SQLite the clause is a no-op (writer locks are database-wide), and joining with it can lock more rows than intended - check the emitted SQL per dialect.
